description: Curious team of students who want to do their best : )
summary: SPHEREx Sky Inspector is a web application that turns NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey (0.75–5 µm, 102 colour bands) into something anyone can explore. SPHEREx’s raw archive is a huge set of small exposures, each seeing only a thin slice of colours. Users pick any spot on an Aladin Lite sky map, and within minutes the server downloads the exposures from NASA/IPAC IRSA and builds a 102-plane spectral cube for each observation epoch. It then compares epochs, measures stars with calibrated photometry, and automatically flags variable stars, infrared-excess objects, “orphan” sources with no Gaia counterpart, and moving-object candidates. This addresses the challenge of finding what changes in the sky by adding, subtracting and blinking images taken at different times, and by comparing SPHEREx with older surveys (DSS2, 2MASS, WISE). It matters because it makes a very large public dataset usable by both students and researchers, with full provenance and exports.
details:
What it does / how it works

  • The user selects a field of 3′–8′ (or any position via name or coordinates).
  • The server queries IRSA for every SPHEREx exposure crossing the field across all data releases. It groups them into epochs (a new epoch starts after a gap of more than 60 days) and downloads cutouts in parallel.
  • Each exposure is resampled onto a common 6.15″ grid with normalised interpolation and combined with inverse-variance weights. The result is a 102-band cube per epoch, built progressively in 3 passes so a preview appears early.
  • Epochs are aligned and scaled using the field’s brightest stars. The target itself is excluded so its own motion or variability is not cancelled.
  • Gaia DR3 stars are moved to each epoch’s date and fitted jointly with a PSF model. This gives total flux in µJy and AB magnitude per band and epoch, with errors rescaled using random empty-sky positions.
  • Automatic flags mark variable, ir_excess, orphan, known_asteroid, saturated and artefact.
  • Movers are searched both between epochs and within an epoch (first half minus second half), and matched against known bodies.
  • Compare tools include A−B difference, A+B and all-epoch stacks, blink, fade and curtain.
  • An “Old sky map ↔ SPHEREx” tab measures a star’s proper motion and brightness change against DSS2, 2MASS and AllWISE.
  • A click anywhere gives a spectrum, and a quality panel says how far each measurement can be trusted.
  • A global coverage map shows where SPHEREx has data.

Benefits and intended impact

  • It lowers the barrier to SPHEREx data: no data skills are needed, and guided tours, a glossary and one-click analysis help students and teachers.
  • For researchers it provides calibrated photometry, provenance.json with SHA-256 hashes, FITS/VOTable/CSV export, a REST API, permanent citable links (/r/<id>), and a shared catalogue of unconfirmed candidates.
  • The intended impact is more people exploring SPHEREx, more citizen-science leads (variables, IR-excess objects, mover candidates), and reproducible results.
  • A progressive pipeline shows a preview after the first third of the data.
  • The coverage map spreads each detector footprint (~3.5°) over a 1° grid and renders it with a WebGL2 shader.
  • Blink comparison between SPHEREx and 40-year-old sky surveys makes motion and variability visible by eye.
  • Gaia is used to predict where a fast mover should be in 2MASS or WISE, so it is not confused with a neighbour (for example Barnard’s Star).
  • Provenance, permanent links and a shared candidate catalogue give a reproducible, community-oriented workflow.
  • The same site serves both a student mode and a researcher mode.

Tools, languages, software

  • Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI/Uvicorn, Pydantic, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, reproject, scikit-image, Matplotlib, Pillow, pyvo, astroquery, requests, aiohttp, fsspec.
  • Frontend: vanilla JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Aladin Lite 3.8.2, a WebGL2 shader for the coverage map, IndexedDB for offline copies, and WebSocket presence.
  • Infrastructure: SQLite (WAL) shared store with a worker queue, Docker and Docker Compose (including scaled mode), and Prometheus metrics.

Factors the team considered

  • Honest limits: movers are candidates, not discoveries. Spectra are not simultaneous, so variable stars are averaged over an epoch. Saturated cores and crowded fields are flagged, and the empirical error calibration has not yet been validated against public SPHEREx photometry.
  • Resilience and scale: retries on IRSA errors, backpressure (HTTP 429), rate limits, and job re-queueing if a worker dies.
  • Reproducibility: pinned dependencies and a recorded git commit and code hash.
  • Always-current data: one query over all releases means new weekly SPHEREx data appear with no code change.
  • Accessibility for newcomers: tours of the five challenge targets (Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae, R Draconis).
